questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] knowledge-base ingestion and retrieval for retrieval-augmented chat (organized-study-dify, dify/fable docs/upskill/01-codebase-cartography/05-key-flows.md). Scenario: an AI app platform hosts 30,000 workspaces. One enterprise workspace uploads 40,000 PDFs over a weekend, about 60,000 characters each, and crawls a 5,000-page documentation site; the embedding provider allows 3,000 requests a minute on the platform's key; chat apps answer from the top 4 retrieved chunks with a p95 under 2 seconds; users re-upload edited versions of the same files; and a dataset marked private to its creator must never answer inside a teammate's app. Write your design before you look: how an upload becomes searchable and where its progress is recorded, how one heavy workspace is kept from starving everyone else, how documents are cut into chunks and what the chunk size is measured in, how many embedding calls the weekend costs and how provider limits are handled, how retrieval finds and ranks chunks, how re-uploads avoid duplicate work, and where dataset permissions are enforced. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Split the write path from the pipeline: the request only checks quotas, writes document rows and commits, then hands ids to a worker; the worker flips each document to parsing in a short committed transaction and runs the slow extract, split and embed work outside any transaction, so progress and errors live on the document row itself.

[w3] Fairness per workspace: sandbox and paid plans go to different queues, and within them a per-workspace isolation queue lets one batch run while later batches wait in a Redis list behind a running flag (one at a time by default, with a one-hour expiry), so the 40,000-file weekend cannot starve other workspaces; the flag is read and set as two separate commands, so two simultaneous uploads can both start.

[w3] Size chunks in the unit the model pays for: automatic mode cuts at 500 with an overlap of 50 (the console pre-fills a custom 1,024, and custom rules allow 50 to 4,000), but the splitter measures that limit with the string length, in characters, not tokens. At roughly 450 new characters per chunk, 40,000 documents of 60,000 characters make about 5.3 million chunks.

[w3] Embedding is the long pole: each chunk is looked up in an embedding cache by its text hash, and misses are sent to the provider in slices of the model's declared batch size, one text per call when a model declares none. At one per call, 5.3 million chunks at 3,000 calls a minute is about 30 hours; at 16 per call it is under 2 hours, so batch to the provider's limit and budget the weekend explicitly.

[w2] Provider limits need a retry policy, not just fallback: with several credentials configured, a rate-limited one cools down for 60 seconds and the next is tried, but with a single credential the call is made once, and the indexing tasks themselves have no automatic retry, so one 429 turns a document to error. Put a token bucket per credential in front of the provider and retry with backoff inside the worker.

[w2] Retrieval runs per dataset against its own collection, filtered by the dataset id: semantic, full-text or hybrid, with top 4 and no score threshold by default; hybrid merges the hit lists and reranks them (a rerank model or a weighted score) and deliberately skips the similarity threshold at the vector stage, because embedding similarity is not comparable to fused scores.

[w2] Re-uploads are matched by file name only, and only when the duplicate option is set; there is no content-hash check, and every chunk gets a fresh random id, so re-indexing an unchanged file re-extracts and re-splits it, runs a cache lookup for every chunk and rewrites every vector and segment row. Chunks already carry a text hash, but nothing uses it to skip an unchanged one; hash each document, and skip the chunks whose hash is unchanged.

[w3] Dataset permissions are enforced on the management screens but not where apps are wired and answers retrieved: attaching a dataset to an app checks only that it exists in the same workspace, and retrieval filters by workspace, so a creator-only dataset whose id is known can answer in a teammate's app. Check the permission level when a dataset is attached and again at retrieval.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the enterprise weekend goes wrong. A worker is killed mid-batch, after which the workspace's next uploads sit in 'waiting' for an hour and 37 documents show 'indexing' forever; an admin changes the chunking rule on 2,000 documents and answers start quoting both the old and the new chunks; some answers cite passages that have nothing to do with the question; after documents are deleted, some answers draw on three chunks instead of four; and the paid tier's backlog grows for a day with no alert. What breaks, how does each show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] A dead worker leaves two kinds of debris: the workspace's running flag survives until its one-hour expiry, so queued batches wait for it, and documents whose segments were saved before embedding stay in 'indexing' because nothing sweeps them, and the resume path that embeds only unfinished segments is reachable only through pause and recover, while a manual retry re-runs the whole document. Renew the flag as a heartbeat while work runs, and add a sweeper that re-queues stale documents through that resume path.

[w3] Old and new chunks both answer because the update deletes the old segment rows only when the vector cleanup succeeded, then re-indexes anyway; a failed cleanup leaves the old vectors and rows next to the new ones. Fail the update when cleanup fails, or index the new chunks as a separate version and switch over in one step.

[w3] Unrelated passages come from a misaligned batch: when the provider returns a vector that normalises to NaN it is skipped, and the remaining vectors are paired back to texts by position, so every later text in the call gets its neighbour's vector, and those wrong vectors are written to the cache under each text's hash, poisoning later re-indexes too. Keep the text-vector pairing explicit and fail the batch on a bad vector.

[w2] Three chunks instead of four means orphan vectors: a document's cleanup failure is logged while its rows are deleted anyway, and retrieval drops hits whose segment no longer exists only after the top-k cut, so each orphan costs a slot. Over-fetch before the join, and run a reaper that compares vector ids with live segments.

[w2] The silent backlog is a monitoring gap: the queue monitor checks the length of the 'dataset' queue only, while paid workspaces go to 'priority_dataset'. Alert on every indexing queue and on the age of the oldest waiting document per workspace, not on queue length alone.
[w1] Treat every hop as a trust boundary and re-check quotas in the worker, as the platform already does, because plan limits and vector space can change between enqueue and execution.
keyPoints.quote: the queue is a trust boundary

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your knowledge-base design against the alternatives: per-workspace isolation queues versus one shared queue with priorities; an embedding cache shared across workspaces versus one per workspace; character-sized flat chunks versus token-sized chunks versus parent-child chunks; hybrid search with a rerank model versus a weighted score versus semantic search alone; deleting a disabled chunk's vector versus keeping it behind a filter; and letting a model pick one dataset versus querying them all and reranking. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Isolation queues buy fairness (one heavy workspace waits behind itself) at the cost of throughput for that workspace, since its batches run one at a time by default and 40,000 files can take days; a shared queue with priorities is faster for the whale and unfair to everyone else. The per-workspace concurrency setting is the dial between them.

[w3] The embedding cache is keyed by model, provider and text hash with no workspace column, so boilerplate embedded once is reused by everyone, which saves real money; the cost is that one bad vector poisons every workspace that embeds the same text, and a per-workspace key would trade that blast radius for more provider calls.

[w2] Character sizing is cheap and predictable but maps loosely to model limits; token sizing matches what the model reads and charges, at the cost of a tokenizer call per piece; parent-child chunks embed small children for precise matching and return the larger parent for context, which costs extra storage and, in whole-document mode, makes one document a single parent.

[w2] A rerank model gives the best ordering at the cost of an extra model call per query and its latency; a weighted score is free at query time but forces every dataset in a query onto the same embedding model; semantic search alone is simplest and misses exact terms such as error codes and product names.

[w2] Deleting the vector when a chunk is disabled keeps queries simple and leaves nothing stale to filter, at the cost of re-indexing on re-enable and a compensation step when the delete fails; a filter flag makes toggling instant but every query must carry it and the store keeps growing.

[w1] Letting a model route each question to one dataset saves retrieval work but bets recall on one routing decision; querying all attached datasets and reranking costs more per question and finds answers that span datasets.
